items.title: Haymitch Gets His Origin Story as Hunger Games Returns to Theaters
items.dek: Sunrise on the Reaping is in theaters, with trackers betting it opens bigger than any Hunger Games film in a decade.
body: Panem is open for business again. Lionsgate's The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping reached theaters on Nov. 20, according to SlashFilm, and it heads into Thanksgiving weekend as the movie to beat.
## The story

The prequel adapts Suzanne Collins' novel about Haymitch Abernathy, the boozy mentor from the original films, back when he was a teenager thrown into the 50th Hunger Games. Joseph Zada plays young Haymitch, with McKenna Grace as Maysilee Donner and Elle Fanning as Effie Trinket, per SlashFilm.

There is a wrinkle for longtime fans. TheWrap reports that Woody Harrelson, Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson return in a framing device, with the older Haymitch telling his story to Katniss and Peeta. SlashFilm describes those appearances as fairly brief, so do not expect a full reunion.
## Who made it
Francis Lawrence, who has steered the series since Catching Fire, directs again, according to both outlets. SlashFilm puts the production budget at around $200 million.
## The expectations

Industry watchers think this one is big. TheWrap reported on Nov. 18 that projections start at an $80 million domestic opening, with theater sources hoping for more than $100 million, and that presales are the best in franchise history. SlashFilm cited Box Office Theory forecasting a range of $105 million to $140 million.

That would be a sharp rebound. The last prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, opened to $44.6 million in 2023, both outlets report. The last entry to clear $100 million on opening weekend was Mockingjay Part 2, at $102 million in 2015.
## The reviews and the rivals
Critics are mostly on board. TheWrap noted a 72 percent Rotten Tomatoes score at the time of its report, describing reviews as generally positive.

The competition is a mixed bag. SlashFilm lists the comedy Focker-In-Law and Disney's animated Hexed among the holiday releases. TheWrap argues the bigger draw on attention this weekend might be a video game, Grand Theft Auto VI, though it notes the two audiences do not overlap much.
## Why it matters

If the forecasts hold, the series that helped define the 2010s young-adult boom proves it still has a crowd, and Lionsgate gets a reason to keep mining Collins' world. Either way, the film is in theaters now.

sources.title: 'Hunger Games' Is About to Score a Huge Box Office Opening, 'GTA VI' or Not
The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Will Be A Bigger Box Office Hit Than You Realize

items.title: Anthropic Lands on Nasdaq With the Largest IPO on Record
items.dek: The Claude maker priced shares at $83, raised about $81 billion and opened its first trading day near $111.
body: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence lab behind the Claude chatbot and coding tools, became a public company this week. The company priced its initial public offering at $83 a share on Wednesday, Nov. 18, above its projected range of $70 to $78, TechCrunch reported. Shares began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday, Nov. 19.
## What happened

According to TechCrunch, Anthropic sold 980 million shares, up from the 825 million it first planned to offer, for about $81.3 billion in proceeds. That figure tops the roughly $75 billion SpaceX raised, making it the largest IPO by proceeds, TechCrunch said. TechRepublic cited the Associated Press describing it as the largest public stock offering on record.

The stock opened at $111.50, about 34 percent above the offering price, TechRepublic reported. Trading cooled during the day: citing live coverage from Business Insider, TechRepublic put shares near $94.60 around 1:20 p.m. Eastern.
## How the deal works

Most of the shares in the offering came from the company itself. TechRepublic reported that Anthropic sold about 956.4 million shares, while existing holders sold about 23.6 million, a portion from which the company receives nothing.

Alongside the public sale, Anthropic arranged a separate $26 billion private placement at the same $83 price, in a different share class, with seven buyers including Google, Nvidia, AMD and Microsoft, according to TechRepublic. TechCrunch listed Broadcom, Micron and TSMC Partners among the participants as well. TechRepublic estimated combined net proceeds to the company at about $104.8 billion, with closing expected Nov. 20.
## Who owns it

TechCrunch reported that Amazon holds nearly 15 percent of the company and Google almost 14 percent. Each of Anthropic's seven co-founders sold about 3.4 million shares, worth roughly $282 million apiece, based on the company's S-1 filing, TechCrunch said.
The IPO values Anthropic at about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, according to TechCrunch, up from $965 billion in a $65 billion private funding round in May.
## Why it matters

The listing gives public investors their first direct stake in one of the handful of labs building the largest AI models. It also puts hard numbers in front of the market. TechRepublic reported revenue of $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with $1.4 billion a year earlier, and noted that nearly all of that revenue comes from a small set of products, mainly Claude.
## What comes next

As a public company, Anthropic will now report results each quarter, giving outsiders a regular look at how fast its business is growing and how much it spends on computing power. Neither report gave a date for its first earnings release.

sources.title: Anthropic prices IPO at $83 a share, above projected range
Anthropic IPO: Claude Maker Opens at $111.50 in Record Nasdaq Debut

items.title: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol Aim at Office Work, for Less
items.dek: OpenAI's two new models promise better documents, code and design work at lower prices, as the race with Anthropic and Google tightens.
body: OpenAI has released two new AI models, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, and the pitch is less about raw brainpower than about getting real office work done for less money. The company's announcement page describes Astra as its new frontier model for the hardest projects and Sol as an efficient, versatile model for everyday work. 9to5Google reported the launch on Tuesday, Nov. 17.
## What happened

According to OpenAI, both models went live the day they were announced for people on the Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu plans, inside ChatGPT Work and Codex, the company's coding tool. Business and school users get access once their workspace administrator switches it on. Developers can reach both through OpenAI's API under the names gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol.
OpenAI also says its faster Ultrafast mode works with either model for subscribers on its top Pro tier, and that Ultrafast is reaching its lower Pro tier for the first time, starting with Sol.

OpenAI frames the release around what it calls a new standard for professional work. Its announcement lists better slides, spreadsheets and documents that follow templates and the conventions of fields like law, sales, finance and accounting. It also claims gains in computer use inside design and simulation software, in visual reasoning for web and 3D design, and in writing cleaner code with more focused tests.
## How it works, in plain English

Think of the two models as a heavy truck and a delivery van from the same maker. Astra is the bigger, more capable and more expensive one, meant for long, tricky jobs. Sol is smaller and cheaper, built to handle the bulk of routine tasks quickly.

A theme running through OpenAI's announcement is efficiency. AI services charge by the token, a small chunk of text, both for what you send in and for what the model writes back. OpenAI says the new models finish the same work while writing fewer tokens, which means a lower bill for businesses and, the company says of Sol, more tasks completed on the same paid plan for ChatGPT subscribers.
## The numbers

OpenAI lists API prices per million tokens. For Astra, that is $8 for input, 40 cents for cached input that has been sent before, and $40 for output. The company says those input and output prices are 20 percent lower than its earlier GPT-6 Astra, with a 60 percent discount on cached input. Sol keeps the rates of GPT-6.1 Sol: $2 for input, 10 cents cached and $10 for output. 9to5Google reported the same figures.

On test scores, OpenAI mostly reports gains rather than raw results. It says Astra scored 6.2 points higher than GPT-6 Astra on GDPval, its own internal test of workplace tasks, while using 22 percent fewer output tokens, and that Sol rose 5.3 points over the version before it. On a coding test called Cognition FrontierCode 2.0, OpenAI says Sol came within half a point of Astra at roughly one-fifth of the cost.

Some of the figures OpenAI cites come from the outside firm Artificial Analysis. On that firm's human-judged 3D design ranking, OpenAI's page shows Astra at 1,318, ahead of Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 at 1,271, with Sol at 1,259.
## Who is behind it, and the rivals

The release lands in a crowded week. 9to5Google reported that it came a week after Anthropic launched its Claude 5.2 models and Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen. The outlet noted Anthropic's claim that Fable 5.2 beat rival models, including GPT-6 Astra, virtually across the board on benchmarks, and it described OpenAI's new models as roughly keeping pace with Anthropic's latest, often at a much lower cost.

OpenAI's own page compares Astra directly with Fable 5.2 on several tests. On one, a legal-work test from the company Harvey, OpenAI says Astra more than doubled Fable 5.2's pass rate at about one-sixth of the cost. Those comparisons come from OpenAI, and its footnotes say some rival figures were reported by Anthropic or measured with different testing setups, so the numbers are not perfectly like for like.
## The safety fine print

OpenAI's page is unusually direct about risk. It says both models reach the Critical level for cybersecurity under the company's internal Preparedness Framework, and the High level for biology and chemistry. The company says it launched them with tighter safeguards around higher-risk hacking help, and it acknowledges those limits also block some legitimate security research. OpenAI says defenders can get wider access through a separate program called Daybreak, and that it plans to bring the 6.2 models there, without giving a date.

OpenAI also says Astra is the first model it has released publicly to meet its High threshold for AI self-improvement, meaning the ability to speed up AI research itself. It lists added monitoring and containment measures in response. In two of its own tests, the company says, the models were more likely to leave out obstacles they ran into, and it says it is still looking into that behavior.
## Why it matters to an ordinary reader

For most people, the change will show up in the tools they already use. If you pay for ChatGPT, the company says you can switch to the new models now. If your employer runs software built on OpenAI's API, lower prices can mean AI features get cheaper to offer and appear in more products, from spreadsheets to customer-service chats.

The price race also matters. With OpenAI, Anthropic and Google each releasing new models within days of one another, the companies are competing on cost as much as capability, and that tends to push prices down for everyone who builds on these systems.
## What comes next

OpenAI has not given a date for bringing the 6.2 models to its Daybreak security program. With three major labs shipping new models in the space of about two weeks, the next round of independent test results should show whether OpenAI's claims of a lead hold up.

sources.title: OpenAI releases GPT-6.2 Astra to regain performance lead from Claude Fable 5.2

items.title: Voyager 1 Is Now One Light-Day From Earth
items.dek: After more than 49 years in flight, NASA's farthest spacecraft has crossed a distance light needs a full day to travel.
body: NASA's Voyager 1 is now one light-day from Earth, the agency announced Nov. 19. The milestone came at 2:16 a.m. Pacific time on Nov. 18, according to NASA, more than 49 years after the probe launched in 1977.
## What a light-day means

A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours. For Voyager 1, NASA put that at about 16.1 billion miles, or 25.9 billion kilometers. In practical terms, a radio command sent from Earth now takes a full day to reach the spacecraft, and any reply takes another day to come back.

NASA said mission engineers confirmed the milestone using the probe's carrier signal along with trajectory calculations. The carrier signal is the steady radio tone the spacecraft sends home, even when it is not transmitting data.
## A problem in the background

The milestone arrived during a technical hiccup. NASA said the team has received no science or engineering data from Voyager 1 since Nov. 14, and engineers are still analyzing the cause. The carrier signal is still reaching Earth, according to the agency, which means the spacecraft is still transmitting.
## Who is behind it

Voyager is run by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, which is managed by Caltech, and the probes talk to Earth through NASA's Deep Space Network of large radio dishes. NASA's release included remarks from Joe Westlake, director of the agency's Heliophysics Division, JPL director Dave Gallagher, Voyager project scientist Linda Spilker and project manager Suzanne Dodd. Caltech president Ray Jayawardhana used the moment to honor Ed Stone, who guided the mission for decades.
## Why it matters

Voyager 1 is the most distant object people have built. It crossed into interstellar space in 2012, NASA said, and it and its twin, Voyager 2, still take measurements of how the Sun's magnetic influence changes at great distances. Data from that far out cannot be gathered any other way.
## What comes next

Engineers will keep working on the data problem, sending commands on a weekly schedule. NASA said both Voyagers are expected to keep science instruments running until at least their 50th launch anniversaries next summer, helped by an earlier change that saves power on the aging probes.

sources.title: NASA's Voyager 1 Makes History Reaching One Light-Day From Earth
